debrief.title: CDC checkpoint coupling to activity naming
text: Mapping Data Flow CDC manages state internally by saving a watermark or transaction sequence number in an internal metadata store. Historically, this state is indexed by combining pipeline and activity names.

When an engineer renames a pipeline or activity, the runtime searches for checkpoint state under the new name. Because none exists, ADF assumes this is a greenfield CDC consumer and initiates a full historical read.

debrief.title: Decoupling state with Custom Checkpoint Keys
text: To eliminate this vulnerability, Microsoft introduced the Custom Checkpoint Key property in Data Flow CDC source options. Setting an explicit, static string (e.g. 'merchant_tx_cdc_key') binds the checkpoint to the key.
With a custom key configured, developers can rename pipelines, refactor activities, or reorganize folders without risking checkpoint loss or accidental historical re-reads.

debrief.title: Idempotent sink architecture
text: The secondary failure was caused by using append mode in the Delta Lake sink. When 45 million historical transactions were re-read, they were appended as duplicates.
An idempotent sink using `MERGE INTO` matching on business transaction IDs guarantees that duplicate reads update existing records harmlessly rather than corrupting financial ledgers.

takeaway: By default, Mapping Data Flow CDC checkpoints are coupled to pipeline and activity names.
Always define an explicit Custom Checkpoint Key for production CDC sources to survive refactoring.
Design sinks to be idempotent (Upsert/Merge) so unexpected full reads do not create duplicate records.

check.prompt: What is the architectural difference between Allow Schema Drift and Validate Schema in ADF Mapping Data Flows?
options: Allow Schema Drift validates data types; Validate Schema re-creates the database table

Allow Schema Drift is for SQL sources only; Validate Schema is for CSV files only
check.why: Allow Schema Drift enables dynamic, evolving schemas to flow through transformations without design-time column mapping. Validate Schema enforces strict contract checking, failing the activity if source columns deviate.

check.prompt: If an upstream database modifies an existing column from integer to string, how does a standard Copy activity behave with explicit column mapping?
options: It silently drops the modified column from the destination
It fails during execution because incoming string values cannot cast into target integer types
It automatically alters the destination database table schema
check.why: In Copy activity with explicit column mapping, ADF attempts type conversion according to the configured mapping. If an incoming string cannot be converted into the destination type, the copy activity fails.

check.prompt: What risk arises when schema drift is enabled unconditionally directly into an enterprise reporting data mart?

check.why: Uncontrolled schema drift can introduce breaking schema changes to downstream BI dashboards, or allow newly added sensitive columns (e.g., social security or credit card numbers) to bypass privacy controls.

check.prompt: What is the recommended enterprise architectural pattern for managing schema drift in a lakehouse architecture?
options: Disallow all schema changes across all layers
Allow schema drift into raw/bronze ingestion zones, and enforce strict schema validation and governance into silver/gold zones
Manually rebuild pipelines whenever a new column is added
check.why: A multi-hop architecture allows schema drift in raw ingestion (Bronze/Landing) to prevent pipeline failures, while enforcing strict schema validation, type enforcement, and curation in processed layers (Silver/Gold).

debrief.title: The double-edged sword of Allow Schema Drift
text: Allow Schema Drift is designed to make pipelines resilient to upstream schema evolution by allowing new columns to flow through without requiring manual pipeline redesign.

debrief.title: Multi-hop schema governance (Bronze versus Gold)

In contrast, Silver and Gold curated zones enforce strict schema contracts using Validate Schema or explicit column mappings. Newly arrived drifted columns remain quarantined in raw storage until formally approved and cataloged.

debrief.title: Protecting downstream analytical contracts

scenarios.title: The balances that matched
scenarios.outcome: Row counts and total balances match after cutover, yet individual customers' balances are wrong.

content.bookmark: Matching total row counts and balance sums does not prove migration accuracy; robust reconciliation requires key-level checksums, boundary checks, and discrepancy logging.

check.prompt: Why is comparing source row count against destination row count insufficient to prove data accuracy after a database migration?
options: Row counts in Azure are calculated in base-16 rather than base-10
Matching row counts can mask duplicate inserts that offset missing rows or data corruption
Row counts only measure index size, not data records
check.why: If a pipeline drops 50 rows due to primary key conflicts but inserts 50 duplicate records from a retry, the total row count remains identical while 100 customer records are corrupted.

check.prompt: How can a migration pipeline's total account balance sum match perfectly while individual customer balances are incorrect?
options: Cloud databases automatically balance accounting ledgers
Off-setting errors (e.g. one account +$500 and another -$500, or misaligned account IDs) can result in an identical grand total
ADF Copy activity caches accounting balances across runs
check.why: Aggregate sums only verify the total volume of money, not its distribution. Off-setting negative and positive variance, or shifting balances between customer IDs, leaves the total sum unchanged while individual records are wrong.

check.prompt: What is the third level in a 5-level enterprise reconciliation framework?
options: Manual spreadsheet review
Key-level hash or checksum comparison across business entities
Restarting the pipeline three times
check.why: The 5 levels are: 1) Row counts, 2) Column aggregate sums, 3) Key-level hash/checksum comparisons, 4) Business rule & boundary validation, and 5) Discrepancy exception table logging. Key-level hashes catch individual row corruption.

check.prompt: What operational mechanism should be implemented in ADF before decommissioning a legacy source system?
options: A reconciliation gate that blocks cutover unless key-level variance is zero or formally approved
Deleting the legacy database immediately upon pipeline completion
Setting pipeline timeout to zero
check.why: A formal reconciliation gate queries source and target systems, compares key hashes, and requires zero unexplained variance before production traffic cutover or legacy system decommissioning.

debrief.title: The illusion of macro aggregate validation
text: Row counts and total sums are macro metrics. In this migration, a collation mismatch between mainframe EBCDIC and Azure SQL ASCII caused non-alphanumeric customer ID sorting to misalign.
While total money ($14.8B) and row count (4.2M) matched exactly, balances were mapped to the wrong customer IDs. Macro sums mask off-setting errors and row-level transposition completely.

debrief.title: Implementing the 5-level reconciliation framework
text: A production-grade reconciliation framework must enforce five successive validation gates: Level 1 (row count check), Level 2 (column aggregate totals), and Level 3 (key-level SHA-256 entity checksums).
Level 4 enforces business domain boundaries (e.g. no negative balances on savings accounts), and Level 5 logs all discrepancies into an exception table with automated variance threshold alerting.

debrief.title: Designing a non-negotiable cutover gate
text: Never decommission legacy sources or redirect live traffic based solely on pipeline completion. Production architectures require an automated reconciliation pipeline.
This pipeline executes entity-level hash joins between source and target, outputting a variance report. Cutover sign-off requires verified zero variance across primary business keys.

takeaway: Matching row counts and aggregate balance sums does not prove individual records are correct.
Implement key-level entity hashing (Level 3 reconciliation) to catch swapped or corrupted records.
Enforce an automated reconciliation gate that halts cutover if cell-level discrepancy exceeds zero.

scenarios.title: The bill that doubled
scenarios.outcome: Oversized concurrency and uncoordinated parallel copies double the monthly cost while degrading throughput.

content.bookmark: Unconstrained pipeline concurrency, loop batchCount, and parallelCopies saturate source and sink endpoints, causing connection thrashing, retry loops, and billing surges.

check.prompt: What is the operational difference between ADF pipeline concurrency and ForEach activity batchCount?
options: Pipeline concurrency controls the maximum number of concurrent runs of that pipeline (no default max); ForEach batchCount limits concurrent iterations within a loop (default 20, max 50)
Pipeline concurrency has a hard limit of 5; ForEach batchCount is unlimited
They are identical settings configured in the factory properties
check.why: Pipeline concurrency controls the maximum number of concurrent runs of that pipeline (configured per pipeline with no maximum by default; additional runs queue once reached), which is distinct from ADF service-level concurrent pipeline-run limits across the factory. ForEach batchCount limits concurrent iterations within a loop (default 20, max 50).

check.prompt: In this scenario's architecture, an on-premises database has a stated capacity constraint of a 20-connection pool. If a team sets ForEach batchCount: 50 to copy 50 tables simultaneously, what happens?
options: Throughput increases linearly by 250%
Connection starvation, query timeouts, and retry loops occur, inflating compute duration and cost while degrading throughput
ADF automatically scales the on-premises database connection pool
check.why: Parallelism that exceeds the source database's stated capacity constraint (here, a 20-connection pool limit, which is the scenario's stated capacity constraint rather than an Azure product limit) causes connection throttling and timeouts. Retrying activities consume billable DIUs and IR compute hours while overall data transfer throughput collapses.

check.prompt: What is the architectural difference between Data Integration Units (DIUs) and degree of copy parallelism (parallelCopies) in a Copy activity?
options: DIUs allocate cloud compute capacity (CPU/memory); parallelCopies specifies the maximum concurrent sub-tasks/threads opened by that copy activity
DIUs manage network bandwidth; parallelCopies is only used for Azure Synapse PolyBase sinks
They are identical settings and can never be configured independently
check.why: DIUs provide scalable compute capacity for the Copy activity; the available/configurable range depends on the ADF runtime and scenario (for Azure IR intelligent throughput optimization, current Microsoft documentation describes configurable values from 4 to 256). Degree of copy parallelism (parallelCopies) specifies concurrent sub-tasks/threads opened by that activity. For capacity planning, potential connection pressure follows an upper-bound planning model: (Active Pipelines) × (ForEach batchCount) × (parallelCopies). The effective number of threads/connections can be lower because ADF may dynamically determine effective copy parallelism and connector behavior varies by source/sink.

check.prompt: When diagnosing an ADF pipeline where raising DIUs and loop concurrency fails to improve data transfer speed, what should an architect investigate first?
options: Immediately upgrade the Azure Data Factory to a higher subscription tier
Whether the bottleneck is at the source or sink endpoint capacity (connection pools, DTU/DWU limits, disk I/O, or locks) rather than ADF compute
Convert all Copy activities into Web activities
check.why: Systematic bottleneck analysis examines the end-to-end path. If source database read throughput, connection pools, or sink transaction logs are saturated, increasing ADF compute or loop concurrency only increases queuing, retries, and billable duration.

caseStudy.setting: Global FinTech Analytics runs 400 nightly data ingestion pipelines moving transactional ledgers into an Azure Synapse Analytics warehouse.

events.what: To accelerate ingestion, a performance task force increased ForEach batchCount from 10 to 50 across all pipelines and set Copy activity DIUs to 32 per table.

With 5 master pipelines executing simultaneously (no pipeline concurrency limit) and each Copy activity configured with parallelCopies: 4, the pipelines attempted over 400 concurrent connections against an on-premises database with a 20-connection pool and a shared Synapse sink.

The monthly Azure bill arrived showing ADF compute charges surged from $8,500 to $27,400, while overall nightly batch runtime actually increased by 25 minutes due to connection timeouts, activity retries, and sink lock contention.

pipeline: Master pipeline triggers 5 child pipelines concurrently with default pipeline concurrency (no maximum configured).
Each child pipeline executes a ForEach loop with batchCount: 50 iterating across tables.
Each Copy activity is configured with 32 DIUs and parallelCopies: 4 against an on-premises database with a 20-connection pool.
Synapse Analytics sink suffers transaction log bottlenecks and lock contention under uncoordinated parallel bulk inserts.
tasks: How do pipeline concurrency, batchCount, parallelCopies, and DIUs compound?
How do you perform bottleneck analysis across source, IR, and sink tiers?

debrief.title: The multi-tier concurrency hierarchy: Pipeline, ForEach, and Copy
text: ADF concurrency operates across three distinct levels: 1) Pipeline concurrency controls the maximum number of concurrent runs of that pipeline (configured per pipeline with no default limit; excess runs queue), which is distinct from ADF service-level concurrent pipeline-run limits across the factory; 2) ForEach batchCount controls parallel loop iterations (1 to 50); 3) parallelCopies sets concurrent threads inside each Copy activity, while DIUs provide scalable compute capacity for the Copy activity (the available/configurable range depends on the ADF runtime and scenario; for Azure IR intelligent throughput optimization, current Microsoft documentation describes configurable values from 4 to 256).

As a potential connection pressure / upper-bound planning model, peak connections scale as: (Active Pipelines) × (ForEach batchCount) × (parallelCopies). The effective number of threads/connections can be lower because ADF may dynamically determine effective copy parallelism and connector behavior varies by source/sink. However, as an upper-bound planning model, attempting 5 × 50 × 4 = 1,000 concurrent threads against a 20-connection database pool triggers immediate connection starvation, query timeouts, and retry cascades.

debrief.title: Source and sink capacity: why unbounded parallelism degrades throughput
text: Adding compute cannot overcome endpoint bottlenecks. When parallel copy streams saturate source database connection pools, queries wait in locked queues. Similarly, flooding a Synapse staging sink causes tempdb exhaustion, transaction log throttling, and table lock contention.

Because ADF charges for compute by the minute, activity retries and blocked connection wait states keep Azure IR compute and DIUs actively running on the bill. Concurrency without endpoint capacity planning causes thrashing, resulting in higher costs and slower runtime.

debrief.title: A systematic 5-tier bottleneck analysis and concurrency budgeting framework
text: Systematic bottleneck analysis asks: Is the delay in the queue (pipeline concurrency limit), loop orchestration (batchCount), activity streams (parallelCopies), compute allocation (DIUs), network bandwidth (SHIR), or endpoints (source/sink connection limits, locks, DTU/DWU limits)?

Establish an explicit concurrency budget based on the lowest endpoint capacity: reserve 4 connections for operational queries on a 20-connection source, leaving 16 for ingestion. Budget backwards: pipeline concurrency 2, ForEach batchCount 4, parallelCopies 2 (2 × 4 × 2 = 16 connections max). Size DIUs conservatively (4-8 for small/medium files; 16+ only for partitioned multi-gigabyte tables).

takeaway: Use (Active Pipelines) × (ForEach batchCount) × (parallelCopies) as a potential connection pressure / upper-bound planning model; effective connections can be lower as ADF dynamically determines copy parallelism.
Perform bottleneck analysis before increasing DIUs: if the endpoint is throttled, adding ADF compute only inflates cost.
Establish an explicit concurrency budget based on the smallest bottleneck in the end-to-end architecture.
content.honesty: If you haven't managed an ADF concurrency and cost overrun incident yourself, don't pretend you have. Explain the multi-tier concurrency hierarchy (pipeline concurrency, ForEach batchCount, parallelCopies, DIUs) and how to budget concurrency against source and sink capacity.

check.prompt: What is the exact function of the Secure Input and Secure Output settings on an ADF activity?
options: They encrypt the payload at rest in storage using customer-managed keys

options: Disable logging entirely or enforce strict storage container RBAC, customer-managed encryption (CMK), and automated lifecycle deletion

check.why: PCI-DSS mandates strict controls over Primary Account Numbers (PAN). If session logs contain raw PANs, the storage container falls under PCI audit scope and requires customer-managed keys, strict RBAC, and rapid purging.

check.prompt: Does enabling Secure Input on a Copy activity prevent sensitive columns in rejected rows from being written to the fault tolerance log?
options: Yes, Secure Input automatically redacts storage session logs
No, Secure Input only masks activity monitoring telemetry; storage session logging is an independent data movement feature
Yes, it replaces all digits with asterisks in storage
check.why: Secure Input and Secure Output apply strictly to monitoring and telemetry visibility. They have no effect on data written to target sinks or fault-tolerance storage logs.

caseStudy.setting: Apex Card Services processes credit card dispute transactions from merchant terminal flat-files into an Azure Synapse Analytics data warehouse.

events.what: Merchant POS batch 404 contained 1,200 records with unescaped commas in customer billing notes, causing column misalignment during Copy activity execution.
With enableSkipIncompatibleRow enabled and Secure Input/Output enabled, the Copy activity completed green; 1,200 bad rows were redirected to an ADLS Gen2 session log container.

A routine PCI-DSS audit discovered that the session log container had broad internal developer read permissions, and held 1,200 full 16-digit credit card numbers (PANs) and CVVs in plaintext CSV files.

pipeline: Get Metadata activity retrieves merchant settlement files from SFTP.

debrief.title: The scope boundary of Secure Input and Secure Output
text: Secure Input and Secure Output are strictly telemetry suppression features. They mask input JSON and output JSON in ADF monitoring dashboards and Azure Monitor Log Analytics.
They do not alter data plane operations. Data written by a Copy activity—whether to target tables or to fault-tolerance error logs—is written exactly as received from the source.

debrief.title: The PCI-DSS trap of session logging
text: When Copy activity skips an incompatible row, it captures the complete raw record into the session log so engineers can debug delimiter or type issues. This includes all sensitive columns.

In payment processing, writing raw Primary Account Numbers (PANs) and CVVs into an unencrypted or broadly accessible storage container violates PCI-DSS Requirement 3, incurring severe audit penalties.

debrief.title: Securing sensitive operational error streams
text: To secure sensitive error data, session log containers must be isolated in a dedicated storage account configured with Azure Key Vault Customer-Managed Keys (CMK) and private endpoints.
Access must be restricted via strict Azure RBAC (Storage Blob Data Contributor restricted to automated remediation identities), coupled with automated lifecycle rules that purge logs within 7 days.

takeaway: Secure Input/Output only masks portal and telemetry logs; it has zero effect on storage session files.
Fault tolerance session logs capture complete raw row payloads, including sensitive PII and credit card numbers.
Isolate, encrypt with CMK, restrict with RBAC, and automatically purge all error logging containers.

debrief.title: The Lookup activity 5,000-row ceiling
text: Azure Data Factory enforces a hard limit of 5,000 rows (and 4 MB payload size) on the Lookup activity output. This is a control plane protection boundary that cannot be increased by support requests.

debrief.title: Architecting scalable metadata chunking

debrief.title: Control plane limits versus data plane throughput

content.bookmark: Large-scale migrations require realistic throughput modeling; an 80 TB transfer over 1 Gbps takes over a week in theory and over two weeks in practice, requiring delta synchronization and cutover controls.

check.prompt: What is the theoretical minimum transfer time to move 80 TB of data over a dedicated 1 Gbps network connection running at 100% saturation?
options: Approximately 24 hours
Approximately 7.4 days
Approximately 21 days
check.why: 80 TB = 640,000 Gb. At 1 Gbps (1 Gb/second), continuous transfer takes 640,000 seconds = ~177.8 hours = ~7.4 days. This is pure theoretical throughput with zero protocol overhead or latency.

check.prompt: In real-world enterprise migrations, why does an 80 TB network transfer typically take 14 to 18 days rather than 7.4 days?

Integration runtimes require 12 hours of cool-down per day
check.why: Real transfer throughput will be lower than the theoretical line rate due to protocol overhead, encryption, disk I/O, and concurrent network traffic; architects commonly assume ~50% effective utilization for planning purposes.

check.prompt: In a 3-week migration timeline for 80 TB of active transactional data, how should initial snapshot and delta sync be structured?
options: Shut down the source system for 3 weeks and run one single copy
Perform an initial baseline copy (or physical Data Box transfer) while the source remains live, then run continuous CDC/incremental pipelines to catch up changes before cutover
Copy only the latest 3 days of data and discard historical tables
check.why: Performing a live baseline snapshot followed by continuous incremental CDC synchronization allows the source system to remain operational until a brief cutover window reconciles final deltas.

check.prompt: Why should enterprise migration plans avoid promising 'guaranteed zero data loss'?
options: Data loss is inevitable in all cloud migrations
Defensible architecture defines explicit controls, dual-write verification, and a reconciliation gate intended to prevent data loss rather than unprovable guarantees
Microsoft SLA documents state 5% data loss is standard
check.why: Professional architecture avoids absolute claims. Rigorous designs specify explicit controls, dual ingestion verification, and strict reconciliation gates intended to prevent data loss before decommission.

caseStudy.setting: Horizon Financial Group must migrate an 80 TB core transactional banking data warehouse from an on-premises data centre to Azure Synapse Analytics within a mandatory 3-week regulatory data centre exit.

debrief.title: The physics of large-scale network data migration
text: 80 Terabytes is 640 Terabits (640,000 Gigabits). At a 1 Gbps link speed, 100% mathematical utilization requires 640,000 seconds = ~7.4 days.

For planning purposes, architects assume an illustrative ~50% effective utilization (~500 Mbps) to account for TCP protocol overhead, TLS encryption, source database I/O, and shared corporate traffic, which extends real-world transfer time to approximately 15-17 days.

debrief.title: Phased baseline snapshot and continuous incremental sync
text: A large-scale migration must never rely on a single monolithic copy. The architecture must decouple the historical baseline from live transactional changes.

The baseline snapshot moves in parallel batches (or via physical Azure Data Box appliances), while a lightweight incremental CDC pipeline captures live changes continuously. By cutover weekend, delta catch-up takes minutes rather than weeks.

debrief.title: Defensible cutover controls versus zero-loss guarantees
text: Enterprise architects avoid promising 'guaranteed zero data loss'. Instead, they design a cutover framework with explicit operational controls intended to prevent data loss.
This includes dual-ingestion pipelines, pre-cutover freeze windows, and a multi-level automated reconciliation gate that verifies transaction hash alignment before legacy feeds are decommissioned.

takeaway: Plan network migration timelines based on 50% effective throughput, not theoretical link speed.
Decouple baseline historical snapshots from live delta synchronization to keep cutover windows minimal.
Structure cutover with verifiable reconciliation gates and fallback contingency runbooks.

debrief.title: The 2 MB return value limit for Databricks activities in ADF
text: The Azure Data Factory Databricks Notebook Activity can receive values returned from the notebook via `dbutils.notebook.exit()` for downstream control flow, with a 2 MB size limit. debrief.title: Separation of control flow from bulk data storage

Bulk analytical records must be written directly to Delta Lake or ADLS Gen2 by Databricks Spark writers. The notebook should only return a lightweight JSON summary: `dbutils.notebook.exit(json.dumps({'status': 'SUCCESS', 'flaggedCount': 65000, 'storagePath': 'abfss://...'}))`.

Write transformed data directly to Delta Lake or ADLS Gen2 storage; return only scalar metadata to ADF.
Use dynamic expressions over `@activity('...').output.runOutput` to route control flow based on summary metrics.

Microsoft Fabric is a unified SaaS analytics platform built around OneLake and shared Fabric Capacity (CUs). It simplifies administration and integrates natively with Power BI, but relies on SaaS security models that may not fit strict legacy PaaS network boundaries.

debrief.title: Workload-driven platform selection framework
text: Enterprises should evaluate workloads against three distinct archetypes: 1) Complex Hybrid Ingestion (keep in ADF for deep SHIR and VNet isolation), 2) Algorithmic Data Science & Heavy Compute (leverage Databricks or Synapse Spark), and 3) Unified Analytics & Business Reporting (adopt Fabric for Direct Lake and OneLake governance).
Forklift migrations that rewrite functioning ingestion pipelines deliver zero new business value while consuming millions in migration spend and introducing regression risk.

debrief.title: The OneLake shortcut bridge pattern
text: The strategic architecture bridge between ADF and Fabric is OneLake Shortcuts. OneLake shortcuts can point directly to existing ADLS Gen2 storage containers populated by ADF pipelines.
Fabric lakehouses and Power BI can query these tables instantly via Direct Lake mode with zero data duplication, zero rewrite of ADF pipelines, and zero migration downtime.

takeaway: ADF is not deprecated; it remains Microsoft's premier enterprise PaaS orchestration engine.
Choose ADF for complex hybrid networking and granular private endpoints; choose Fabric for unified SaaS analytics.
Use OneLake shortcuts to connect existing ADF-managed lakes to Fabric without rewriting pipelines.
content.honesty: If you haven't evaluated ADF against Microsoft Fabric in an enterprise architecture review, don't pretend you have. Explain the PaaS versus SaaS trade-offs, capacity billing versus consumption meters, and the OneLake shortcut coexistence pattern.

points: Evaluate migrations based on business outcome: rewriting working pipelines consumes budget without adding features.
Adopt a workload-driven strategy: retain hybrid and complex VNet ingestion in ADF.
Adopt Fabric where unified SaaS analytics, Direct Lake mode, and low-code collaboration add distinct value.
Use OneLake shortcuts to connect existing ADLS Gen2 assets to Fabric without data duplication.

debrief.title: Delivery risks of mass pipeline migration
text: Rewriting 2,400 pipelines requires massive developer capacity, extensive regression testing, and protracted dual-running costs.

debrief.title: Structuring hybrid delivery waves
text: Wave 1: Connect Fabric OneLake to existing ADLS Gen2 storage via shortcuts and build new reporting products.
Wave 2: Build greenfield cloud-native pipelines directly in Fabric where SaaS integration is advantageous.
Wave 3: Retain existing hybrid on-premises ADF pipelines in maintenance mode.

Structure phased delivery: pilot Fabric for reporting while maintaining ADF for operational ingestion.
Leverage OneLake shortcuts to unlock Fabric capabilities immediately without migration overhead.
Upskill data engineers incrementally on Fabric workspace governance and Lakehouse architecture.

diagnostic_questions.question: How would you prove a data migration is complete, beyond matching row counts?
points: Counts on every load, per table and per partition or day.
Column profiles compared: totals, minimum, maximum, distinct and empty values.
Row fingerprints (hashes) joined on the key for critical tables, because totals can match while rows differ.
Business rules checked, for example no negative balances.
For money, truncation switched off and totals compared at full precision.
An owner who signs off, and a rule for what happens on a mismatch.

diagnostic_questions.question: A bank is moving customer and card data to Azure. What would you require before any pipeline is built?
points: Where data may be processed: an Azure integration runtime in the required region.
The encryption-key decision made first: a customer-managed key can be set at factory creation or, later, only on an empty factory, and can't be removed once on.
Credentials in Key Vault or managed identities, never in pipelines.
Sensitive values kept out of logs and monitoring: skipped-row logs contain real values when the session log is on; secure input and output on activities.
An agreed masking approach, including whether it may call an external service.
Compliance scope checked, for example PCI DSS, which ADF's own list doesn't mention.

diagnostic_questions.topic: Keeping source and target in sync
diagnostic_questions.question: How would you keep a migrated table in sync with a source that still receives updates and deletes until cutover?
points: A watermark can't see deletes; change data capture reads inserts, updates and deletes from the source's change log.
An initial snapshot, then changes until cutover.
Loads that are safe to repeat: merge on the key.

The change-capture checkpoint can be lost when what it is keyed to changes (Microsoft documents pipeline and activity names, and newer activities may use a GUID): set your own checkpoint key and rehearse a rename.
A reconciliation at cutover before the old system is switched off.

diagnostic_questions.question: How would you know your data pipelines are healthy, and not just showing green?
points: A green run can mean the error handler succeeded: check the data, not only the run status.
Checks per load or per window, such as row counts, that fail loudly.
An alert on failed runs sent to whoever is on call.
Run history kept beyond ADF's 45 days, in Log Analytics.
A named owner per pipeline, and a way to rerun from the failed step.

diagnostic_questions.question: A nightly load failed part-way through. How would you recover, and how would you make the next failure easier to recover from?
points: Rerun only what failed: from the failed activity, one time window, or one partition.
Make sure the rerun can't duplicate: loads that upsert or replace their window, since ADF may rerun activities itself.
Know what resumes: only binary file copies between file stores resume; every other copy starts again.
Retries set on activities and tumbling windows (the default is none), and alerts to whoever is on call.
Reconcile before calling it fixed, and tell the people who rely on the data.
For a region outage: the factory lives in one region, so keep it in Git and CI/CD to redeploy elsewhere.

diagnostic_questions.question: A nightly load has become too slow to finish on time. How would you approach it?
points: Start from the slowest run: read ADF's performance tuning tips, then find the longest stage.
Match the fix to the stage: a queue means runtime capacity; time to first byte means the source query; listing means file filters.
Change one thing at a time and measure again; the automatic settings are usually best.
Know the knobs: DIUs (Azure runtime only), parallel copies, database partitions, staging, cluster size and time to live for data flows.
Weigh the cost: more speed means more DIU- or vCore-hours, or more load on the source system.

diagnostic_questions.question: How would you release data pipeline changes from development to production safely?
points: Git only on the development factory (Microsoft's recommendation); changes through pull requests.

A build or release pipeline that validates the factory and produces ARM templates (the Publish button's adf_publish branch, or the automated utilities package), deployed to test and production with approvals and one parameter file per environment.
Production changed only through the pipeline, never by hand: recommended practice, not something ADF enforces.
Triggers stopped before a deployment and restarted after, because deploying over active triggers can fail.
Publishing includes the whole factory (no selective publish), so a hotfix route and feature flags for unfinished work.

diagnostic_questions.question: How would you plan the migration of several hundred tables and a large data lake to Azure?
points: A control table listing every table or partition, its load pattern and status: it is also the progress report.
Large data partitioned (Microsoft's HDFS guide says above 10 TB in native mode) so a failure reruns one slice, not everything.
Throughput proven with a proof of concept before dates are promised: the slowest of source, network and target sets the speed.
Online or offline transfer, decided by size, bandwidth and the migration window.
A snapshot plus incremental loads until cutover, and the self-hosted runtime treated as production infrastructure.

diagnostic_questions.question: How would you estimate and control what a data integration platform on Azure Data Factory costs?
points: The main cost drivers, which Microsoft lists as meters plus other charges: orchestration activity runs, copy power (DIU-hours), data flow compute (vCore-hours, including debug sessions), pipeline and external activity time, factory operations, and SSIS runtime hours.
Estimates from a proof of concept, not guesses.
Debug sessions watched: they are billed.
Per-pipeline billing switched on to charge costs back to each team.
Separate factories cost nothing extra: billing is by use.

diagnostic_questions.question: Would you build new data pipelines in Azure Data Factory or in Microsoft Fabric today, and why?
points: Microsoft calls Fabric Data Factory the next generation of ADF.

What changes: connections instead of linked services and datasets, Dataflow Gen2 (Power Query based, with Spark-based mapping data flow transforms in preview) for dataflows, the on-premises gateway, capacity pricing.
What isn't there yet: Azure-SSIS and managed virtual networks.
The ways to move: mount the existing factory, the upgrade tool, or rebuild by hand.
The decision weighs the existing estate and its runtimes against capacity pricing and the missing features.
